title: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?  - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief explains that the Belém-Antalya mechanism (BAM) for a just transition, agreed at COP30, is expected to launch at COP31 in Antalya but its functions and financing remain disputed between developed and developing countries. Proponents argue it is low cost, while the UNFCCC faces a funding gap after the US withdrawal.

insights.claim: The just-transition concept originated in the 1980s from alliances between US labour unions and environmental justice groups and entered the Paris Agreement preamble in 2015.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The idea has a long institutional lineage, which helps explain its broad political support.

insights.claim: COP27 launched a work programme on just transition, but talks at COP29 closed without agreement, and COP30 then agreed to establish a new institutional mechanism, the BAM.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Progress came in fits, so COP31 delivery is far from assured.

insights.claim: Civil society pushed for a mechanism because two dialogues and one ministerial a year under the work programme could not deliver just-transition strategies on the ground.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The BAM is designed to move from talk to implementation, which is the core test.
insights.locator: The idea of the mechanism emerged

insights.claim: Developed countries including Norway and the UK initially opposed the G77 and China mechanism proposal over duplication and funding concerns, and the EU suggested an 'action plan' instead of the term mechanism.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Developed-country resistance on cost and wording foreshadows COP31 bargaining.
insights.locator: Developed countries also opposed the use of the term

insights.claim: Civil society proposals converge on a three-part BAM, such as a steering body with knowledge and implementation arms, with 'rather broad consensus on the functions' but parties pushing in very different directions on setup.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Structure, not purpose, is the likely sticking point in Antalya.
insights.quote: there is “rather broad consensus on the functions”
insights.locator: What role could the mechanism play

insights.claim: Developed countries want the work programme to focus on domestic workforces, while some nations want a global outlook including support for transitions in developing countries.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: This split over scope underlies the finance fight and would shape flows to emerging markets.
insights.locator: Broadly, developed countries would like it

insights.claim: The UNFCCC faces a funding gap after the US withdrawal and delayed or reduced contributions from other parties, leading to cancelled events and unfilled positions, which makes some parties hesitant to create another mechanism.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Institutional budget stress limits the appetite for new mechanisms regardless of the merits.
insights.locator: The push to launch the BAM comes at a time

insights.claim: Proponents say the BAM need not be a costly new institution, citing the Climate Technology Centre and Network as a similar body costing less than $10m a year.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The low-cost framing is the main counter to funding objections.
insights.locator: What are the financial implications of the mechanism?

insights.claim: ITUC says it is not asking for a new just-transition fund and instead wants all climate finance to be just-transition proof.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The labour demand targets existing finance flows, which could add conditionality to climate funds.
insights.quote: “we’re clearly not asking for a new [just-transition] fund, we want all climate finance to be just-transition proof”
insights.locator: What are the financial implications of the mechanism?

insights.claim: Bonn in June 2026 agreed only a 'skeleton' draft text, so many BAM details must be settled in Antalya, and swift approval of the COP31 agenda is described as crucial.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Little negotiating time remains and delays would push launch beyond COP31.

insights.claim: AOSIS, LDCs and the African group back the BAM with an implementation focus, the EU supports it as complementary to the work programme, no submissions opposed it, and LDCs flag 'means of implementation' as a key point.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Broad support suggests launch is likely, with finance the main risk to ambition.

insights.claim: CAN has called for a first face-to-face meeting of a just-transition committee in April 2027 as part of getting the BAM running.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A concrete date shows what civil society sees as a realistic start timetable.
insights.locator: In a submission to the UNFCCC earlier this year

insights.claim: Climate Action Network's Rosemberg says a question mark remains over the ambition of the COP31 presidencies, who must move from talking about establishing any mechanism to one fit for purpose.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Presidency leadership is a swing factor, and a weak mechanism is a plausible outcome.
